evidence: src/application/create-user-use-case.ts: CreateUserUseCase.execute throws `new ApplicationError("name is required", 400)`. That builds the HTTP 400 status into the application layer, and choosing the status is a transport/infrastructure job.
src/infrastructure/user-controller.ts and src/infrastructure/http-server.ts use CreateUserUseCase. They are the right place to turn application errors into HTTP status codes.
Everything else in execute() is application orchestration: ids.next(), new User(...), users.save(user), and mapping to the UserOutput DTO.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Most of CreateUserUseCase.execute is ordinary application-layer work. It checks the input at the use-case boundary, builds a domain User through the injected IdGenerator, saves it through the domain UserRepository port, and maps the result to a UserOutput DTO. That much fits the application layer. The problem is the validation failure: the use case throws `new ApplicationError("name is required", 400)`. 400 is the HTTP "Bad Request" status code. Choosing a transport status code is a presentation/transport (infrastructure) job. It belongs in the HTTP controller or server (UserController / http-server), which should turn application errors into HTTP responses. Putting it here ties the use case to HTTP. This is a fairly small leak, and it would be acceptable if ApplicationError's numeric code were a neutral error code that only happens to match HTTP. That is why confidence is moderate. A smaller point: the "name is required" check could be read as a domain invariant that User should enforce. Input validation at the application boundary is still acceptable, though, so it is not flagged.
